h1: Meter Bank Replacement for Apartment Buildings in Broward County
intro: When a meter bank fails, it is not one unhappy tenant, it is a whole building without power and a property manager whose phone will not stop. The meter bank is the row of meter sockets that feeds every unit, and when it corrodes, burns, or is damaged, the whole building can go dark at once. We know this work and the pressure that rides with it. Our largest recent contract was a ten-meter socket bank replacement on a building that had lost power for a week after a vehicle fire damaged the service equipment. We had the building back online within two weeks of the incident, with the electrical work itself completed in one week. That is the kind of job we are built for: licensed, coordinated, and fast. We show up whenever you call.

definition.heading: What a meter bank is and why it matters
definition.body: A meter bank is the ganged assembly of meter sockets that serves a multi-unit building, one position per apartment, all fed from a common service. Because every unit runs through that one assembly, the meter bank is a shared point of failure: when it corrodes, overheats, or is damaged, it can take power from many units or the entire building at once. In older South Florida buildings these banks have weathered decades of heat, humidity, and salt air, and the metal that carries the load corrodes over time. Replacing a meter bank is major service-side work that requires utility coordination, permitting, inspection, and a crew that can move quickly without cutting corners. For a property manager, it is one of the higher-stakes electrical jobs a building can face.

symptoms.title: Multiple units lost power at once
symptoms.body: Several apartments, or the whole building, went dark together while the neighborhood still has power. When many units fail at the same time, the fault is usually at the shared service or the meter bank, not inside any single unit.

symptoms.title: Rust and corrosion across the bank
symptoms.body: The meter bank shows rust streaks, pitting, or chalky corrosion spreading across the enclosure and around the sockets. Salt air and humidity eat at the metal that carries every tenant's load, and widespread corrosion means the whole bank is aging out.

symptoms.title: Scorching, heat, or a burning smell
symptoms.body: Scorch marks, melted spots, or a hot plastic smell anywhere on the bank mean connections are arcing under load. On a shared assembly feeding many units, that is a serious fire risk that needs a licensed electrician right away.

symptoms.title: Damaged service after an impact or fire
symptoms.body: A vehicle strike, a fire, storm damage, or vandalism has physically damaged the service equipment or the meter bank. When the assembly is compromised, the building may be unsafe and dark until it is properly replaced, which is work we handle.

symptoms.title: Loose, tilted, or missing meters
symptoms.body: Meters in the bank sit crooked, wobble, or have gaps around them, and covers are cracked or missing. Worn sockets no longer grip the meters tightly, which causes arcing and heat and lets moisture into a live assembly feeding many homes.

symptoms.title: The utility red-tagged the equipment
symptoms.body: The power company flagged the meter bank as unsafe or will not reconnect until it is replaced. On a multifamily building that means many tenants stay without power until a licensed electrician replaces the bank and it passes inspection.

localSections.heading: Aging apartment stock and original service
localSections.body: A large share of Broward County's rental housing was built from the nineteen sixties through the eighties, and many of those buildings still run on close to their original service equipment. Meter banks that were installed when the building went up have now carried load through forty or fifty South Florida summers, feeding window units, ranges, and water heaters for unit after unit, year after year. Metal fatigues, jaws loosen, and connections that were tight at installation work loose under decades of heating and cooling. On a single home that slow decline affects one family; on an apartment building it sits above every tenant at once. That is why so many multifamily electrical emergencies here trace back to a tired meter bank rather than anything inside a unit. When we assess an older building, we read the whole assembly and the service behind it, and we tell you honestly whether a targeted repair will hold or whether the bank has reached the end of its service life.

localSections.heading: Heat, humidity, and salt air on a shared assembly
localSections.body: The same climate that wears out a single meter socket is even harder on a meter bank, because a bank has many positions, many connections, and a large expanse of metal exposed to the weather. Humidity is constant, and near the coast salt air corrodes the enclosure, the jaws, and the lugs across every position. Meanwhile the cooling load in an apartment building runs most of the year, so the assembly carries heavy current for long stretches, and corroded or loose connections turn that current into heat. Heat accelerates the corrosion, corrosion adds resistance, and resistance makes more heat, a loop that runs faster on a heavily loaded bank than on a lightly used home. The result is that multifamily service equipment in this region ages hard and can fail across several positions at once. We replace banks with equipment rated for our conditions and make every connection properly, because on a shared assembly a weak point becomes many tenants' problem.

localSections.heading: Permitting and inspection for multifamily work
localSections.body: Replacing a meter bank on an apartment building is significant service-side work, and in Broward County it is permitted and inspected as it should be. For a property manager that oversight is protection, not red tape. A permitted, inspected bank replacement documents that a licensed contractor did the work to code and that an independent inspector confirmed it, on the very equipment that feeds every tenant. We pull the permit under our own license, coordinate the inspection with the utility reconnect, and the owner personally meets the inspector rather than handing it to a stranger. On multifamily property the paperwork matters even more than on a single home, because ownership changes, refinances, and insurance reviews all scrutinize the electrical service, and unpermitted work on a shared assembly is exactly the kind of thing that surfaces at the worst time. We keep the record clean so the new bank stands as a documented asset on the building, not a liability waiting to be discovered.

localSections.heading: What insurance carriers watch on multifamily
localSections.body: Insurance carriers scrutinize apartment buildings closely in South Florida, and the electrical service is near the top of the list. A corroded, scorched, or damaged meter bank is a visible hazard that an inspector or adjuster will flag, and on multifamily property the stakes are higher because many households are exposed. If an electrical fire or failure ever traces back to the service equipment, the carrier will ask whether the bank was replaced by a licensed contractor and whether the work was permitted and inspected. Unpermitted or unlicensed work on a shared assembly is the kind of finding that can slow a claim or put coverage at risk across the whole building. When we replace a bank we do it under our license, coordinate the utility and the permit, and leave documented, inspected work behind. For a property manager, that clean licensed record is part of protecting the owner and keeping the building insurable, and it is handled as a normal part of the job.

guide.title: The complete guide to meter bank replacement for South Florida apartment buildings

sections.heading: What a meter bank is and why it is high-stakes
sections.body: On a single-family home there is one meter and one socket, but an apartment building needs to measure each tenant's electricity separately while still being fed by one service, and the meter bank is how that is done. It is a ganged assembly, a row or grid of meter positions, one per unit, mounted together and fed from common bus work behind them. Each tenant's meter plugs into its own position, but they all share the same incoming service and the same physical assembly. That shared design is exactly what makes a meter bank high-stakes for a property manager. When one socket in a single home fails, one family is affected. When a meter bank corrodes, overheats, or is damaged, the failure can spread across several positions or take down the common bus that feeds the entire building, so a single point of trouble becomes many dark units at once. The assembly also carries far more total load than any home socket, because it is serving many households simultaneously, which means the heat and stress on the equipment are correspondingly greater. Understanding that a meter bank is both a shared point of failure and a heavily loaded one explains why its warning signs deserve fast, licensed attention rather than a wait and see approach.

sections.heading: A real job: ten meters back online in a week
sections.body: The best way to understand what this work involves is a real example, and our largest recent contract fits. An apartment building had lost power for a week after a vehicle fire damaged the service equipment, taking out the meter bank that fed the units. A week without power in South Florida is a crisis for a property manager: tenants with no air conditioning, no refrigeration, and mounting pressure, and an owner who needs the problem solved without an open-ended bill. We took on the ten-meter socket bank replacement, coordinated the utility and the permit, put our crew on it, and completed the electrical work itself in one week, with the building back online within two weeks of the incident. That job is a fair picture of what a bank replacement demands: an accurate assessment of fire-damaged service, tight coordination with the power company for the disconnect and reconnect, a crew that can move on a large assembly, permitting and an inspection done right, and a number the owner could approve without a fight. We share it not as a promise about your building, because every situation is different and the site visit comes first, but as an honest example of the scale and the speed we are built to handle when a building is dark and the clock is running.

sections.heading: Why meter banks fail on older buildings
sections.body: Meter banks fail for the same reasons single sockets do, only multiplied across many positions and accelerated by heavier load, and on older South Florida apartment buildings the causes stack up. Corrosion leads the list. The assembly lives outdoors in constant humidity, and near the coast salt air settles into every jaw, lug, and seam, corroding the metal that carries each tenant's electricity. Heat is the second driver, coming both from the climate and from the current itself, because an apartment building runs cooling loads most of the year and a heavily used bank carries that current for long stretches. Corroded and loose connections have higher resistance, resistance makes heat, and heat speeds the corrosion further, a cycle that runs faster on a loaded multifamily assembly than on a quiet home. Age is the third factor: much of Broward's rental stock is decades old and still on original service equipment that has weathered forty or more summers. On top of all that sit the sudden events, a vehicle strike, a fire, a storm, or water intrusion, any of which can damage a bank that was already worn. Because these forces act on every position of a shared assembly, an older bank tends to fail broadly rather than politely at one meter, which is why replacement, not endless spot repair, is often the honest answer.

sections.heading: How a bank replacement is planned and performed
sections.body: Replacing a meter bank on an occupied building is a coordinated operation, and knowing the sequence helps a property manager plan and set tenant expectations. It begins with a thorough on-site assessment: we examine the full bank, every position, the common bus behind it, and the service feeding the building, and we determine exactly what must be replaced and whether the damage has reached the conductors or the main service. Then you get one honest, forecast-based price that includes the utility coordination and the permit, a number you can take to the owner for approval. Scheduling comes next, and it is where experience counts, because the power company must disconnect the service before the bank can be safely removed, and on a multi-unit building that outage affects many tenants, so the window has to be planned carefully and communicated clearly. Our in-house crew, backed by three trucks, removes the old assembly and installs a new bank with equipment rated for our climate, making every connection to code across all positions. The work is inspected, the owner personally meets the inspector, and once it passes the utility reconnects the service and the meters are reset. Throughout, our aim is to keep the outage as short as safety allows, because on multifamily property every extra hour without power is felt by every household in the building.

sections.heading: Utility coordination and permitting on multifamily property
sections.body: Two things make a meter bank replacement go smoothly instead of turning into a mess, and both are the contractor's responsibility to manage: utility coordination and permitting. The meters and the service belong to the power company, so replacing the bank requires a scheduled disconnect, the licensed work, an inspection, and then a reconnect, in that order. On an apartment building this coordination is more involved than on a home, because more is at stake in the outage window and the utility's process has to line up with the inspection and the crew's timeline. We manage that whole chain so the property manager is not left negotiating with the power company or juggling schedules. Permitting is the other essential. Service-side work on multifamily property is permitted and inspected in Broward County, and that oversight protects the owner: it puts a licensed contractor and an independent inspector on record for the equipment that feeds every unit. We pull the permit under our license and the owner meets the inspector in person. Skipping either step to save a day is a false economy on any building and doubly so on multifamily, where an unpermitted change on a shared assembly can surface at sale, at refinance, or in an insurance review and create a problem far larger than the day it saved.

sections.heading: Choosing a contractor a property manager can rely on
sections.body: A meter bank replacement is one of the more demanding electrical jobs a building can face, and for a property manager the choice of contractor is really a choice about accountability under pressure. Start with licensing, because service-side multifamily work requires it: you want a Florida Certified Electrical Contractor with statewide authority and a Broward County Master Electrician, so the person doing the work is answerable to the state and knows how the local utility and building department operate. Ask whether the company can actually staff a full bank replacement or whether they are a single truck that will string the job out; the ability to put real hands on a large assembly matters when a building is dark. Ask how they handle the utility coordination and the permit, and whether an in-house crew or an unknown subcontractor does the work. Ask how they price, because a property manager needs one honest number to bring to an owner, not a figure that drifts upward mid-job. Ghost Crown Electric has run for ten years, holds 286 permitted projects on public record, stays in the top tier of Florida contractors by permit quality, and runs three trucks so a big job gets real crew. The owner takes the call, prices the job, and meets the inspector personally, so from the first call to the final reconnect, the person accountable for the work is the person you are talking to. Speed without accountability is worthless, and accountability without speed is useless to a building full of tenants, and this company is built to bring both.

sections.heading: Keeping tenants and owners informed through the work
sections.body: On multifamily property the electrical work is only half the job; managing the human side of an outage is the other half, and it is where a property manager either looks organized or looks caught off guard. Because a bank replacement means the building or a block of units is without power during the disconnect, the crew's timing has to line up with what tenants are told, and we help you set those expectations honestly. Before the work day we walk you through the plan: when the power goes off, roughly how long the window should last, and what has to happen with the utility and the inspector before it can come back. That lets you give tenants a straight answer instead of a guess, which keeps complaints down and trust up. We keep you updated as the job moves, so if the utility or the inspection shifts the timing, you hear it from us first and can relay it. For the owner, we provide the documented, permitted, inspected record of the work, which protects the building at the next sale, refinance, or insurance review. Restoring power fast matters, but doing it in a way that keeps everyone informed is what makes a hard day feel handled, and it is a large part of why the property managers who call us once tend to call us again.

faqs.question: Should I repair one bad meter position or replace the bank?
faqs.answer: It depends on the assembly. If the corrosion, heat damage, or age is spread across the bank, replacing one position just moves the problem, and on older buildings the whole assembly is often at the end of its life. We assess the full bank and the service, then give you a straight recommendation so you are not paying to patch something that will fail again.
